title: What is G1 String Deduplication (`-XX:+UseStringDeduplication`), and how does it differ from String interning?

s1_definition.profdef: G1 String Deduplication is a garbage-collector feature, enabled with `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` on the G1 collector, where the collector detects two distinct String objects that hold identical character content and makes them share a single backing character array. The String objects remain separate, but their internal value arrays are merged, saving the memory of the duplicate array. String interning, by contrast, is an application-level mechanism via `String.intern()` that returns a single canonical String object from a pool, so the String objects themselves become identical and the `==` reference comparison returns true.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India prints the branch name "National Bank of India, Mumbai" on millions of passbooks. With String deduplication, each passbook is still its own physical booklet, but the printing press notices the branch line is identical everywhere and stores that line once in a shared ink plate that every passbook points to, saving ink. With interning, you go further: you throw away the duplicate booklets entirely and hand every customer the exact same single master booklet, so when two customers compare booklets they are literally holding the identical object. Deduplication quietly shares the contents behind the scenes; interning merges the whole object and changes identity.
s1_definition.oneliner: Deduplication shares the character array behind duplicate String objects automatically during GC without changing identity; interning returns one canonical String object so even `==` matches.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** G1 String Deduplication is a garbage-collector feature, enabled with `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` on the G1 collector, where the collector detects two distinct String objects that hold identical character content and makes them share a single backing character array. The String objects remain separate, but their internal value arrays are merged, saving the memory of the duplicate array. String interning, by contrast, is an application-level mechanism via `String.intern()` that returns a single canonical String object from a pool, so the String objects themselves become identical and the `==` reference comparison returns true.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India prints the branch name "National Bank of India, Mumbai" on millions of passbooks. With String deduplication, each passbook is still its own physical booklet, but the printing press notices the branch line is identical everywhere and stores that line once in a shared ink plate that every passbook points to, saving ink. With interning, you go further: you throw away the duplicate booklets entirely and hand every customer the exact same single master booklet, so when two customers compare booklets they are literally holding the identical object. Deduplication quietly shares the contents behind the scenes; interning merges the whole object and changes identity.

**One line to remember:** Deduplication shares the character array behind duplicate String objects automatically during GC without changing identity; interning returns one canonical String object so even `==` matches.

sections.s2_technical:
A Java String is a small object wrapping a backing array of characters, which since Java 9 is a byte array under compact strings. When an application reads the same text many times from different sources, for example parsing the same currency code or status word out of millions of messages, it creates many separate String objects that each own their own identical copy of the character data. The String objects are cheap, but the duplicated character arrays can waste a surprising amount of heap. Studies by the JVM team found that duplicate strings often account for a significant percentage of the live heap in typical server applications.

G1 String Deduplication tackles this transparently inside the collector. When G1 processes strings during young collections, it computes a hash of each String's character array and checks a deduplication table. If it finds another String whose array has the same content, it redirects the newcomer's internal value field to point at the already-existing array and lets the duplicate array become garbage. Crucially, the two String objects stay distinct objects at different addresses; only the backing arrays are unified. This means the feature is completely invisible to application semantics. No `equals` result changes, no `==` result changes, and no code needs modification. You simply add `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` and the heap shrinks for duplicate-heavy workloads. The deduplication work happens on a background path tied to the collector, so it does not block application threads directly, and it respects an age threshold so only strings that survive a while are considered, avoiding churn on short-lived strings.

String interning is a different, older, application-visible mechanism. Every String literal in source code is automatically interned by the compiler and class loader into the string pool, which lives in the regular heap in modern JVMs. Calling `String.intern()` on a String at runtime looks up the pool: if an equal string is already present, it returns that canonical instance; otherwise it adds this string and returns it. The effect is that two interned strings with equal content are the same object, so `s1 == s2` is true, not just `s1.equals(s2)`. Interning therefore saves memory like deduplication, but it also changes object identity, which enables fast reference comparison. For example, if you intern account status codes, you can compare them with `==` instead of `equals`, and in the finance domain code you might write `if (statusA.intern() == statusB.intern())`.

The differences that matter in an interview are as follows. Deduplication is automatic and controlled by the JVM flag, requires no code change, keeps String objects distinct, and only merges the backing arrays; it is a garbage-collector optimization. Interning is explicit and controlled by the application calling `intern()` or by using literals, merges the whole String object into a canonical instance, makes `==` work, and is managed by the application. Deduplication is safe to turn on broadly because it cannot change behaviour. Interning must be used deliberately, because over-interning can bloat the pool and because relying on `==` for strings is a well-known bug when some strings are not interned. In practice, a banking service dealing with millions of repeated codes often turns on deduplication for a free heap win and uses interning only in narrow, controlled hot paths where reference comparison genuinely helps.

The senior nuance is that deduplication costs some collector CPU and table memory, so you validate the trade-off with `-Xlog:stringdedup` to see how much it actually saves, and that interning the wrong strings, such as high-cardinality unique values like transaction identifiers, is harmful because it fills the pool with entries that never repeat.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India ingests millions of transaction messages per hour, and every message carries repeated text fields such as the currency code "INR", the channel "UPI", and the status "SETTLED". Each message is parsed into objects, and the heap fills with millions of separate String objects holding the identical words. The service runs out of heap even though the distinct vocabulary is tiny. This is exactly how duplicate strings waste memory: the same few words are copied millions of times into separate backing arrays.

Problem 2 — The team wants two things: a free, zero-code-change heap reduction for the general case, and a fast reference comparison in the hot status-routing path where the same status is checked billions of times. This is exactly the division of labour between deduplication and interning: deduplication gives the broad automatic saving, while interning gives the narrow `==` speedup where it is deliberately applied.

We will build a runnable demo that simulates parsing many transactions, shows how many duplicate status strings are created, demonstrates interning collapsing them into one canonical object so `==` becomes true, and explains where G1 deduplication would transparently share the arrays. The code includes a Transaction object holding a status string, a StatusRouter that compares statuses, an Interner wrapper, and a demo main that contrasts naive equals comparison, interned `==` comparison, and notes the deduplication flag.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run with G1 String Deduplication ON (transparent heap win)
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:+UseStringDeduplication -Xlog:stringdedup -jar target/txn-ingest-service-1.0.0.jar

# The stringdedup log prints bytes saved and strings deduplicated
# Interning is in the code itself; no flag needed for intern()
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transactions, both parsed with the status text "SETTLED" created via `new String(...)` so each is a distinct object with its own backing array.

Step 1: The two transactions hold two separate String objects. A reference comparison with `==` on the raw statuses returns false, because although the content is equal, the objects live at different addresses and own different character arrays.

Step 2: The StatusInterner calls `intern()` on each status. The first call finds "SETTLED" already present in the pool because it is a literal elsewhere, and returns that canonical instance. The second call returns the same canonical instance.

Step 3: Now a reference comparison with `==` on the interned statuses returns true, because both references point at the single canonical object. The duplicate objects are eligible for collection.

Step 4: The StatusRouter uses the fast path, comparing the canonical status against the interned literal "SETTLED" with `==`, which is a single pointer comparison and returns true.

Step 5: The safe path demonstrates that `"SETTLED".equals(status)` still returns true on the raw, non-interned string, proving the safe comparison does not depend on interning.

Step 6: The demo logs that for the broad heap win across millions of messages, enabling G1 String Deduplication shares the backing arrays automatically with no code change, while interning remains the deliberate tool for the hot `==` routing path.

```
2026-10-30 17:48:40 INFO    Raw statuses == ? false (distinct objects, duplicate arrays)
2026-10-30 17:48:40 INFO    Interned statuses == ? true (one canonical object)
2026-10-30 17:48:40 INFO    Fast == routing says settled? true
2026-10-30 17:48:40 INFO    Safe equals routing says settled? true
2026-10-30 17:48:40 WARNING For the BROAD heap win across millions of messages, run with -XX:+UseStringDeduplication on G1 — it shares arrays with ZERO code change.
```

```text

    │
    ├─ DEDUPLICATION (GC, -XX:+UseStringDeduplication)
    │    String A ─┐
    │    String B ─┼→ G1 finds equal content → share ONE char[] 
    │    String C ─┘   (objects stay distinct, == still false)
    │    result: heap shrinks, semantics unchanged
    │
    └─ INTERNING (app, String.intern())
         "SETTLED" copy 1 ─┐

         "SETTLED" copy 3 ─┘   (objects merged, == now TRUE)
         result: == works, fast routing
    ▼
  StatusRouter: == (interned) OR equals (always safe)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
G1 String Deduplication and String interning both attack the same waste, which is many separate String objects holding identical text, but they work at different levels and have different effects. A String is a tiny object wrapping a backing character array, and when a server parses the same words out of millions of messages it creates millions of separate objects each owning its own copy of that identical data, which can consume a large slice of the heap.

G1 String Deduplication is a garbage-collector feature you turn on with the UseStringDeduplication flag on the G1 collector. During collection, G1 hashes each String's backing array, and when it finds two distinct Strings with identical content it redirects one to share the other's array and lets the duplicate array become garbage. The key property is that the String objects stay distinct objects at different addresses; only the backing arrays are merged. That makes the feature completely invisible to application behaviour, so no equals result changes, no reference comparison changes, and no code needs modifying. It is a free heap win for duplicate-heavy workloads, paid for with a little collector CPU and a deduplication table.

String interning is an older, application-visible mechanism. Every literal in source code is interned automatically into the string pool, and calling intern at runtime returns the single canonical instance for that content, adding it if absent. Because interning merges the whole String object, two interned strings with equal content are literally the same object, so a reference comparison with the double-equals operator returns true. Interning therefore saves memory and additionally enables fast reference comparison, but it changes object identity and must be used deliberately.

In a project at National Bank of India we ingested millions of transaction messages carrying the same few status words, and the heap filled with duplicate status strings. We used both tools for their strengths. We enabled G1 String Deduplication globally for the broad, zero-code heap reduction, since it cannot change semantics and simply shrinks the live set, and we confirmed the saving with the stringdedup log. Then in the one hot status-routing path, checked billions of times, we interned the status words deliberately so we could compare them with the double-equals operator as a single pointer comparison instead of a full character equals. The rule I always state is that deduplication is automatic, keeps objects distinct, merges only the arrays, and is safe to turn on broadly, whereas interning is explicit, merges the whole object, makes reference comparison work, and must be reserved for low-cardinality repeated values, never for unique identifiers like transaction numbers that would only bloat the pool.

---

keyPoints: G1 detects duplicate String values on the heap and shares the backing char[]
Different from intern(): dedup works on ANY String, not just interned ones
Saves memory for applications with many duplicate string values
Trade-off: adds GC overhead for scanning — measure before enabling
